planting.note: Transplant container-grown plants after the last frost into fertile, well-drained soil in partial shade to bright filtered light; also thrives as a potted houseplant since its stem cuttings root easily even in water.

directions: Firebrand produces upright canes of glossy, lance-shaped leaves in a reddish-purple base color crossed by noticeably paler, contrasting veins, a pattern that sets it apart from solid dark cultivars such as Black Magic. Grow it in partial shade with bright, filtered light; deeper shade mutes the vein contrast while intense midday sun can scorch the leaf margins. Plant in fertile, humus-rich, well-drained soil and water regularly enough to keep the root zone evenly moist without waterlogging, reducing frequency in cooler months. Because young stem cuttings root readily, Firebrand is easy to propagate and is also popular as a foliage accent in humid indoor plantings and paludariums, though garden specimens should stay out of standing water.

planting.note: Transplant after the last frost into fertile, well-drained soil in partial shade; give it room to reach its larger mature size compared with most ti plant cultivars.

directions: Negra is one of the larger-growing ti plant selections, forming a multi-caned shrub whose long, strap-like leaves emerge deep burgundy and darken toward near-black as they mature in bright light. Provide partial shade with strong filtered sun; too little light causes the foliage to green up, while harsh, unshaded midday sun can bleach or scorch the dark pigment. Grow in rich, well-drained, slightly acidic soil kept evenly moist through the growing season, and let the surface dry slightly between waterings in winter. Because of its bold height and dark color, Negra works well as a dramatic backdrop planting or large container specimen paired with lighter-colored tropical foliage for contrast.

common_name: Maria Ti Plant (Pink and Burgundy Variegated Cordyline)

planting.note: Transplant after the last frost into fertile, well-drained soil in partial shade to bright filtered light for the strongest pink streaking.

directions: Maria carries glossy, lance-shaped leaves streaked in bold combinations of hot pink, burgundy, and green over a rich purple base, making it one of the showiest multicolor ti cultivars in cultivation. Site it in partial shade with bright, filtered light; stronger light intensifies the pink streaking, while low light shifts the balance toward plain green and purple. Plant in fertile, well-drained soil and water often enough to keep it consistently moist, since this cultivar is less drought-tolerant than plain-leaved ti plants. Use Maria as a specimen accent in shaded tropical borders or large containers, and bring potted plants indoors well before nighttime temperatures drop into the 40s Fahrenheit.
sources: North Carolina State University Extension Gardener Plant Toolbox

common_name: Hawaiian Flag Ti Plant (Pink, Cream and Maroon Striped Cordyline)

planting.note: Transplant after the last frost into fertile, well-drained soil in partial shade; allow ample vertical space since this is one of the taller-growing striped ti cultivars.

directions: Hawaiian Flag produces bold, broad leaves striated in pink, cream, green, and maroon, a busy multi-tone pattern that darkens slightly as the foliage ages. Grow it in partial shade with bright, filtered light to keep the stripe colors vivid without scorching; deep shade dulls the variegation. Plant in fertile, well-drained soil and water regularly to maintain even moisture, tapering off in cooler months when growth slows. Its tall, upright canes make it a good vertical accent at the back of a tropical border or as a tall specimen in a large patio container.
sources: North Carolina State University Extension Gardener Plant Toolbox

common_name: Miss Andrea Ti Plant (Cream, Pink and Olive Variegated Dwarf Cordyline)

planting.note: Transplant after the last frost into fertile, well-drained soil in partial shade to bright filtered light; the compact habit suits mixed containers as well as garden beds.

directions: Miss Andrea is a compact ti plant selection bred in Florida, prized for broad, recurving leaves irregularly striped in olive green, cream, soft pink, and purple with a pale leaf margin. Grow it in partial shade with bright, filtered light for the clearest variegation; too little light causes the pastel tones to fade toward plain green. Plant in fertile, well-drained soil and keep it evenly moist during active growth, allowing the soil surface to dry slightly before watering again in winter. Its shorter, denser habit compared with standard ti plant cultivars makes it well suited to mass plantings, mixed tropical containers, or as a colorful mid-border accent.
sources: Fairchild Tropical Botanic Garden Plant Shop

common_name: Curly Merry Christmas Rex Begonia (Spiral-Leaf Sport)

planting.note: Grow as a houseplant or shaded container plant year-round; move outdoors to a sheltered, shaded spot only after nighttime temperatures stay reliably above 55 degrees Fahrenheit.

directions: Curly Merry Christmas is a spiral-leaved sport of the classic Merry Christmas rex begonia, arising from a creeping rhizome and producing medium-sized leaves whose bases twist into a tight coil before flaring outward, echoing its parent's pink-and-green zoned coloring in a whorled form. Grow it in bright shade to indirect light in humus-rich, well-drained potting mix, keeping the soil evenly moist but never soggy. Water at the soil line rather than overhead, since wetting the curled leaf bases encourages rot and fungal spotting in the tightly furled new growth. Maintain humidity above 50 percent and steady warmth, and divide the rhizome to propagate new plants once a clump fills its container.

common_name: Ring of Fire Rex Begonia (Red-Rimmed Silver-Veined Begonia)

planting.note: Grow as a houseplant or shaded container plant; move outdoors to sheltered deep shade only once nighttime temperatures stay reliably above 55 degrees Fahrenheit.

directions: Ring of Fire is a vigorous, full-mounding rex begonia hybrid whose serrated, angel-wing-shaped leaves show a bold red rim and center set against silver patterning over deep green veins, an effect that intensifies in cooler weather and softens somewhat during summer heat. Grow it in bright, indirect light in humus-rich, well-drained soil, watering enough to keep the mix lightly moist and letting it approach a slight wilt between waterings rather than staying saturated. Keep humidity above 50 percent and nighttime temperatures above 60 degrees Fahrenheit for the best leaf color and to prevent stress-related leaf drop. Its larger, more vigorous habit compared with compact rex cultivars makes it well suited to hanging baskets or wide, shallow containers where the mounding foliage can spread.
